entry.title: Marie Kondo, Dunbar’s Number, and Non-Existence as a Means of Knowledge
entry.content:
In this post, we relate Marie Kondo's book on tidying up, Dunbar's number, and non-existence (abhava in Sanskrit [1]) as a means of knowledge.

Marie Kondo's book on tidying up [2] has two interesting and, in our opinion, main observations:

  1. One must keep items that spark joy when one is in a calm state of mind and holds the items in one's hands.
  2. The items that are discarded using the method above give us knowledge about what we did not understand about ourselves—that is, which items we thought we would like at the time of purchase but did not end up liking.

First, we observe that both of these observations involve emotions; i.e., we keep the items that spark commonly positive emotions and reflect on the commonly negative emotions inspired by the discarded items.

Now, we analyze these observations using only the mind; that is, we remove emotions (i.e., the body and senses) from them and look at them only from the point of view of the mind.

Dunbar's number is defined as follows [3]:

Dunbar's number is a suggested cognitive limit to the number of people with whom one can maintain stable social relationships—relationships in which an individual knows who each person is and how each person relates to every other person.

For observation #1 by Marie Kondo, Dunbar's number tells us that we have a cognitive limit as to how many people one can maintain stable relationships with. We observe that this is due to a limitation of the mind, similar to [4][5]. So, when observation #1 is viewed only from the point of view of the mind, it becomes the cognitive limit on how many products one can remember and use consistently without forgetting about them. We have simply replaced relationships with people with relationships with products in Dunbar's number's definition.

For #2 by Marie Kondo, we recall the idea of non-existence as a means of knowledge that we discussed in a previous post and have written about extensively [6][7][8]. When we look at it from the point of view of the mind, #2 is essentially saying that the non-existence (abhava) of the discarded items can be a means of knowledge. This would be the Vedantic school's interpretation[6] of Marie Kondo's two observations, in our opinion.

Thus, in this post, we made observations from Marie Kondo's book on tidying up and tried to understand them using only the mind, relating them to Dunbar's number and non-existence as a means of knowledge.

entry.title: On Enlightenment and the Two Interpretations of Perceived Reality
entry.content:
In this post, we argue that the two ways of characterizing perceived reality change the definition of enlightenment.

As we mentioned in a previous post, perceived reality can be characterized as a cognitive bias when the mind is disconnected from the body and the senses[1], and perceived reality is to be understood by the mind alone, without the body and senses.

When perceived reality is not considered a cognitive bias, we end up with an interpretation of enlightenment that is caused by detachment from material things. That is, we are born attached, then become detached, and reach enlightenment. Of note here is that both attachment and detachment assume the presence of emotions towards the material world. We have previously noted that this definition leads to Maya being the mother of Buddha[2].

When perceived reality is characterized as a cognitive bias, and we start analyzing enlightenment only from the point of view of the mind, there cannot be any emotions assumed, and we get a definition that is based on knowledge and the lack thereof, i.e., ignorance. So, the definition of enlightenment becomes a change in the state of the mind from ignorance to knowledge. We observe that this change is similar to how the definition of sin changes[3]. So, according to the following definition from Advaita Vedanta[4], the individual is born enlightened but mistakenly identifies themself with the body and senses:

In a popular sense, [A]dvaita is often expressed as the famous diction that Atman is Brahman, meaning that jivatman, the individual experiencing self, is ultimately pure awareness mistakenly identified with body and the senses, and non-different ("na aparah") from Ātman/Brahman, the highest Self or Reality; the knowledge of this true identity is liberating.

We further guess that this difference is due to the fact that the 'means of knowledge'[5] (Pramana) for Bauddha philosophy and Vedanta philosophy, of which Advaita Vedanta is a part, are different:

Thus, in this post, we argue that the definition of enlightenment depends on whether perceived reality is characterized as a cognitive bias or not.

entry.title: On Non-Existence as a Means of Knowledge
entry.content:
In this post, we make a note of non-existence[1] (abhava in Sanskrit) being a means of knowledge in the Bhatta[2] and Vedanta schools of thought[3] from a commentary on the Nyaya Sutra[4].

We have extensively written and elaborated on the idea of non-existence being the origin of things because of how our mind works, i.e., our mind creates an abstract representation in order to analyze things[5][6]. This can be stated in another way: the non-existence of something can be a means of knowledge. We were pleasantly surprised to find this as a means of knowledge in Satish Chandra's commentary on the Nyaya Sutra[7]:

Thus, in this post, we noted an interesting observation about non-existence being a source of knowledge from Satish Chandra's commentary on the Nyaya Sutra.

entry.title: On Sin
entry.content:
In this post, we argue that the two ways of characterizing perceived reality change the definition of sin.

As we have discussed in a previous post, perceived reality can be characterized as a cognitive bias if the world is understood using only the mind[1]. We believe that this fundamentally changes how sin is understood.

When perceived reality is not characterized as a cognitive bias, an individual is represented by their physical body[2]. When this happens, we attach emotions to sin, and sin is typically considered to be bad or immoral.

When perceived reality is considered a cognitive bias and the world is understood as an abstraction using only the mind, and an individual is represented by an abstraction, there cannot be any emotions attached to sin; there can only be artifacts of the mind attached to it, i.e., knowledge or the lack of it. Thus, sin is understood as acting in a state of ignorance, or lack of knowledge. This, we believe, is why the Sanskrit word pāpa, when understood from the point of view of Advaita Vedanta, is simply acting in ignorance, which essentially has no emotions attached to it and is defined from the point of view of the mind. We couldn't find an authoritative definition of sin, but here's the best we found[3].

Sin, in Vedantic terms, is essentially ignorance (avidyā) of one's true nature, which leads to inappropriate actions. It's not an inherent flaw or a stain on the person, but rather a misunderstanding that causes mental disturbance and unaligned behavior.

Thus, in this post, we argue why the definition of sin as characterized in Vedantic terms is different from how it is characterized by other religions[4]. We note that our understanding is based on intuition rather than study.

entry.title: On Word Distance in Natural Languages
entry.content:
In this post, we discuss an aspect of natural languages, specifically English. We also note that we only make observations about the written aspect of languages, not of the spoken aspect. We call this concept "word-distance" and define it similarly to how it is defined in computer science [1]:

Given two words, A and B, what is the distance between their meanings that warrants their existence as separate words?

We keep the metric of measuring distance vague, but believe there must be ways to quantify it using Mathematics. We now define some common ways in which words with almost zero word-distance exist in languages like English:

  1. Context: We observe that some languages like English have different words that exist for different contexts even when they have the same meaning. For example, the word awesome in a casual context would be translated to impressive in a more serious context, although the distance between them is only contextual.

  2. Synonyms: Another way low word-distance can be introduced is via synonyms. Many times, synonyms can be used in the same context. For example, a synonym for awesome can be amazing, and both can be used in a casual context.

  3. Time[2]: Words can get out of fashion and become dependent on time, like thrice is no longer used; it is three times now.

  4. Space[2]: Even if the language used is the same, separation by space can create different new words for the same meaning. For example, in American English the word tap is not used; it is called faucet.

For a language that describes Nature, like Math is for Physics, we believe that it should be very clear what the word-distance between any two words A and B is. And possibly, there should be some way to quantify meaning. For a language for Physics, the only context is that of Nature, and synonyms just add noise to the language, so the above-mentioned ways can be avoided. Additionally, using different words at different times and in different places can add unnecessary noise.

We note that our observations are only from the point of view of the mind and may be valid for philosophy and science. From the point of view of the body and senses, i.e. for poetry and emotional expression, we believe that the existence of words that can be used interchangeably does provide colorfulness to the language. We have previously written about a perfect language[2], sound[3], and ether[4] that are related to this post.

Thus, we proposed an idea of word-distance based on meaning and made a few observations as to how low word-distance words add noise in scientific and philosophical contexts.

entry.title: On East and West
entry.content:
In this post, we discuss an important distinction between Eastern and Western cultures. We note that by East, we mean how historically the East has been associated with spirituality and the West with materialism, but we believe that the contemporary East and West cannot be characterized by their historical meanings.

As we wrote in a previous post, when perceived reality is understood only through the mind, it can be characterized as a cognitive bias, and empirical truth then has to be modelled differently[1][2][3]. This, we believe, is a fundamental difference between Eastern and Western cultures. The spirituality in the traditional East stems from the assumption of characterizing perceived reality as a cognitive bias, or mithya (untruth) as a result of the force of Maya in Advaita Vedanta and other Eastern religions[4].

Thus, we put forth a hypothesis as to what distinguishes the historical concepts with which the Eastern and Western cultures are associated.

entry.title: On an Aspect of Empirical Truth
entry.content:
In this post, we argue that the definition of empirical truth inherently implies that perceived reality is not a cognitive bias[1].

We first define empirical evidence and assume that empirical evidence is used to arrive at empirical truth[2]:

A thing is evidence for a proposition if it epistemically supports this proposition or indicates that the supported proposition is true. Evidence is empirical if it is constituted by or accessible to sensory experience.

The important idea to note is that empirical truth needs sensory input, i.e., it's not arriving at the truth using only the mind; it's using the body and senses as well in order to arrive at the truth. Thus, it assumes that perceived reality is not a cognitive bias[1].

We believe assuming perceived reality to be a cognitive bias is a central assumption in texts like Advaita Vedanta[3], where the force of Maya is the cosmic force that makes us believe that perceived reality is not a cognitive bias. This assumption leads to a difference in how we define concepts like sound[4][5] from the traditional scientific definitions.

Thus, we argue that the definition of empirical truth inherently makes an assumption that is contrary to texts like Advaita Vedanta, i.e., it does not characterize the perceived reality as a cognitive bias. We qualify that our knowledge of this aspect of Advaita Vedanta is based on intuition and not study. Furthermore, we take a guess that the concept of empirical truth is what distinguishes between Shruti and Smriti[6].

entry.title: On the Life of An Astronomer Hermit and Astrology
entry.content:
In this post, we hypothesize how astrology might have come into existence as a natural consequence of a hermit living alone for a long time in Nature with the aim of coming up with a theory as to why prominent events occur at specific times. This hermit would be similar to that in Thanu Padmanabhan's Akbar story. Note that we make absolutely no claims about the efficacy of astrology whatsoever.

Imagine a hermit, H, living in a hut and interacting only with Nature. In addition, imagine H to have a good knowledge of astronomy. H's aim is to try to come up with a theory as to why prominent events happened in their past at specific times. When H's mind analyzes the events happening around them and those that have happened to them and to others in the past, the only movement they know is that in the Nature around them and that of the planets via their knowledge of astronomy, that's the only sense of Time they have.

It's in the nature of the mind to start correlating planetary motion with the events that have happened in their own lives and those in the lives of others, because H is not aware of any other movement other than the planetary movement known via the mathematics of astronomy and the movement in the Nature around them. This may be how astrology came into existence.

Thus, we hypothesize that it's in the nature of the mind of a knowledgeable hermit to correlate planetary motion known via mathematics with prominent events, if their aim is to come up with a theory to explain why prominent events occur at specific times.

entry.title: On Sound in Nyaya Sutra
entry.content:
In this post, we clarify our understanding of what sound is in texts like Nyaya Sutra[1][2]. Previously, we hypothesized that Shruti is heard via ether[3]. We have also written about how the perceived reality can be characterized as a cognitive bias[4]. We use these two ideas to hypothesize our understanding of sound (shabdah).

We first give the traditional scientific understanding of sound and contrast it with what we believe is the understanding in texts like Nyaya Sutra.

The scientific understanding[5] is to characterize sound as a pressure wave, with frequency being the parameter that determines whether the wave can be heard by the human ear or not. The ear converts the pressure wave to an auditory signal that is sent to the brain.

Now, we contrast this with what we believe is sound as characterized by Nyaya Sutra. As we have written about how perceived reality can be characterized as a cognitive bias[4], we believe that when everything is to be understood with only the mind, we would need to define the ear in an abstract manner, that is, as a concept. So, the concept of the ear is that it provides input to the mind. Now, with this understanding, all auditory input that the mind can understand is from the ear, irrespective of whether it can be heard by others or not. So, sound is not a pressure wave with this understanding; it is what the mind can interpret as coming from the concept of the ears. The physical ears that we have become the physical manifestation of the concept of the ears. And sound becomes what the mind can interpret as auditory input, and it may or may not be a pressure wave or be heard by others.

Thus, we have explained what we believe is sound as characterized by texts like Nyaya Sutra.

entry.title: On Ether
entry.content:
In this post, we hypothesize about how Shruti is heard [1]. We first define sound. We define sound as what is heard by the human ear and interpreted by the mind. That is, we don't define it as a pressure wave requiring a physical medium, but define it from the point of view of the human ear.

We argue that sound has two manifestations, the physical and the abstract, and two mediums of travel, the physical and the ether. Characterization of sound as a pressure wave is the common scientific understanding. In this post, we argue that sound could also have an ethereal character if defined from the point of view of the human ear.

First, we note something about the ears. We observe that it is scientifically known that the sense of sound is active even in deep sleep [2]. In a previous post, we proposed an experiment to characterize perceived reality as a cognitive bias [3]; we refer to this state of mind as S. We hypothesize that the mind in S is similar to deep sleep as far as the sense of hearing is concerned, and that the sense of hearing is still intact in S, although the physical manifestation of sound is absent, i.e., we are in a silent place.

We hypothesize that we hear sound when we are in a state of deep concentration, and the mind remembers it when we come out of the state. This can be easily seen in day-to-day life. When someone is deeply concentrating on something like a computer program or a book, and someone says something to them, they hear it but don't react to it immediately, and react to it after they are out of the state of deep concentration, a few seconds or a fraction of a second later.

This is what happens when our mind is meditating in deep concentration: the sense of hearing is intact, and we remember what we were hearing via ether when we come out of the concentration. We believe that this is how Shruti is heard, via ether. We also note that in texts like the Nyaya Sutra, the sense of hearing is connected to ether, not air [4].

Thus, in this post, we argued how Shruti is heard from ether.
